blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Critical-Path Latency**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Economics, § Critical-Path Latency
blocks.md: Accelerating a model call rarely yields a proportional reduction in end-to-end task time. In realistic agent workflows, container provisioning, repository setup, test suite execution, tool I/O, and consensus validation often dominate total elapsed time. Evaluating an acceleration technique therefore requires an end-to-end view. It must measure how much wall-clock time the proposed change strips from the critical path to a declared endpoint, what compute and memory resources it consumes, and whether the accelerated execution preserves the required acceptance evidence.

questions.q: The section **Critical-Path Latency** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.
Speculative decoding pays only when the accepted-draft rate shortens the output-bound critical path by more than draft and verification work add to the bill.

Every budget account in the tree keeps budget = settled + reserved + free under atomic, logged transitions, so a delegation tree conserves spending and a stopped child keeps its reservation until its late bills settle.

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.
